list.listitem: Diagnosis of alcohol intoxication is made by history and physical examination. A positive blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is helpful to secure the diagnosis but does not correlate with the degree of intoxication or self-perceived intoxication. C
Patients with isopropyl alcohol intoxication have an osmolar gap without an anion gap acidosis. C
Treatment of alcohol intoxication/poisoning is largely supportive. Intubation and mechanical ventilation are sometimes required, but hemodialysis is rarely indicated. C

background.definition: Alcohol is a psychoactive drug that alters brain chemistry. As the BAC rises, slurred speech, ataxia, stupor, coma, and eventually death may occur. Isopropyl alcohol may be taken as an alcohol substitute by alcohol-dependent persons or by those attempting self-harm.

list.listitem: Age-adjusted rates of alcohol-induced deaths generally increased from 2000 to 2020 but rose more rapidly from 2019 to 2020, increasing by 26% during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic (from 10.4 to 13.1 per 100,000 standard population).

Deaths from excessive alcohol use in the United States from 2016-2021 show a 29.3% increase over this time period with approximately two thirds of these deaths resulting from chronic causes during each period.
In 2020, rates of alcohol-induced deaths in both men and women increased with age, peaking in the 55–64 age group.

From 2019 to 2020, alcohol-related deaths increased, including deaths from alcohol-induced acute pancreatitis (increased 50%, from 0.1 to 0.2), mental and behavioral disorders due to use of alcohol (increased 33%, from 3.0 to 4.0), and alcoholic liver disease (23%, from 6.4 to 7.9).

Despite ongoing efforts to mitigate excessive drinking deaths, the average annual estimates of alcohol-attributable deaths and years of potential life lost (YPLL) were slightly higher in 2010-2015 than in 2006–2010, with excessive drinking leading to an average of 95,158 deaths (261 per day) and 2.8 million YPLL (29 years lost per death, on average) in the U.S. annually.

Across all U.S. states in 2020, prevalences ranged from 30.9% to 66.6% for alcohol consumption (at least one alcoholic drink in the last 30 days), 4.4% to 9.9% for heavy drinking (adult men having more than 14 drinks per week or adult women having more than 7 drinks per week), and 11.2% to 22.8% for binge drinking (males having five or more drinks on one occasion or females having four or more drinks on one occasion) using data from the CDC's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System of telephone surveys.
Data from the 2016 National Health Interview Survey (NIHS) showed that 31.6% of men and 18.6 % of women reported at least one heavy-drinking day in the past year.

Among U.S. adolescents, the prevalence of binge drinking declined from about 41% in the 1970s to 1980s, to 28% 1992, and to 17% in 2015 (12th graders). However, the overall proportion of youth participating in binge drinking remains high and increases with age during adolescence.
Between 2006 and 2014, the total cost of alcohol-related U.S. ED visits increased 272% from $4.1 billion to $15.3 billion.

Heavy alcohol consumption and high-risk drinking has been associated with a higher prevalence of injury in women (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.32, 4.66), and scores of 20 or greater on the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) have been associated with a higher prevelance of injury in both women and men (aOR 3.71, 95% CI 2.07, 6.66 and aOR 1.43, 95% CI 1.00, 2.02, respectively).
On simulated driving tests, alcohol consumption significantly increased both standard deviation of lane position and speed, and higher BAC levels were associated with larger performance decrements.
Injuries and fatalities are significantly greater in alcohol-impaired motor vehicle collisions when the BAC level is ≥0.08 g/dl.
Alcohol intoxication is a risk factor for recurrent traumatic brain injury.

Alcohol and the associated sequela of its excessive use affect women differently than men, including sexual violence and complications during pregnancy (such as iscarriage, stillbirth, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders)

Compared to non-intoxicated patients with fractures, intoxicated patients demonstrate a higher rate of head/neck fractures (skull 23.2% vs. 5.8%) and face/orbit fractures (30.4% vs. 9.5%), a lower rate of extremity fractures , and only intoxicated patients presented to the emergency department (ED) with head/neck fractures more than 24 hours old.
Alcohol intoxication and poisoning are a direct result of alcohol consumption where the BAC exceeds the liver's capacity to metabolize the psychoactive substance.
Alcohol overdose/poisoning is intoxication to the point of nausea/vomiting, altered mental status, and/or respiratory compromise.

Isopropyl alcohol intoxication occurs as a direct result of ingesting isopropanol-containing products for the intoxicating effect or to cause self-harm. Many household products such as mouthwashes, hand sanitizers, and cosmetics contain quantities of ethanol sufficient for inducing intoxication.
Based on male twin registry data, familial/social factors are especially important influences for alcohol use, while genetic/temperamental factors are more critical for alcohol use disorders.

With respect to genetic susceptibility, a meta-analysis found strong evidence for an association between an allele of alcohol dehydrogenase 1C and alcohol use disorders. The strongest and most consistent effects were seen in Asian populations.
Rapid consumption of alcohol exceeds the liver's capacity to metabolize alcohol.
At a BAC between 0.25 and 0.40 g/dL, slurred speech, ataxia, stupor, and coma can occur.
Some suggest that the mean fatal BAC is 0.50 g/dL, but there is wide variation of tolerance of high BACs.

Alcohol intoxication results in a marked reduction in brain glucose metabolism (especially in the cerebellum and occipital cortex) and significantly increased brain uptake of acetate as a possible alternate energy source.
Acute alcohol intoxication is associated with slight increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and with left ventricular contraction abnormalities.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Coexisting medical condition (heart disease, liver disease, diabetes)
Use of medications or other drugs
Early physical maturation in girls, especially with low parental supervision

list.listitem: United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening and behavioral counseling interventions to reduce unhealthy alcohol use by adults, including pregnant people, in primary care settings. B
USPSTF does not recommend for or against screening and behavior interventions to reduce or prevent unhealthy alcohol use in adolescents in primary care settings. B
Preventive measures against accidental ethanol or isopropyl alcohol ingestion should include stressing proper storage of toxic materials. C
USPSTF recommends screening and behavioral counseling interventions to reduce unhealthy alcohol use by adults, including pregnant people, in primary care settings.
USPSTF does not recommend for or against screening and behavior interventions to reduce or prevent unhealthy alcohol use in adolescents in primary care settings.

Screening adolescent trauma victims for alcohol intoxication should be considered. In one database study of patients under age 18 years in Los Angeles, 4,899 patients (26.3% of the total population) underwent BAC screening and 57.1% screened positive.
Preventive measures against accidental ethanol or isopropyl alcohol ingestion should include stressing proper storage of toxic materials.

Interventions for college students that challenge alcohol expectancies were helpful in reducing alcohol use and frequency of heavy drinking, but the effects were not maintained at follow-ups greater than 4 weeks. Similarly, an internet-based course with five modules provided to freshman was helpful for short-term reductions in past-30-day alcohol use and binge drinking in the fall semester that did not persist into the spring semester.
State-level alcohol policies that raise alcohol prices and reduce its availability reduce binge drinking.

In an analysis of the potential benefits of alcohol interlock installation in all new US vehicles, investigators estimated that 85% of crash fatalities (>59,000) and 84-88% of nonfatal injuries (>1.25 million) attributed to drinking drivers would be prevented.

Drug therapy to prevent return to use is adjunctive. Data is mixed on the benefit of using disulfiram 250 mg to 500 mg every morning to improve abstinence. Naltrexone reduces alcohol craving and heavy drinking in persons with an alcohol use disorder but does not increase overall abstinence rates.

The opioid receptor blocker nalmefene is only minimally effective in stopping or lessening alcohol use in overuse, with a decrease in the number of heavy drinking days by approximately 1.65 per month (95% CI 0.89-2.1) and no influence on quality of life or short-term mortality. .

Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily increases length of abstinence particularly in those who have had alcohol detoxification or in motivated patients with a treatment goal of abstinence, although this was not reproduced in a recent family medicine-based randomized controlled trial (RCT).
Gabapentin 1800 mg 3 times daily demonstrated a 17% abstinence rate (p = 0.04 for linear dose effect; NNT = 8) and a 44.7% no heavy drinking rate (p = 0.02 for linear dose effect; NNT = 5).

Topiramate titrated over 6 weeks to 200 mg daily reduced heavy drinking in a 12-week RCT with 138 heavy drinkers. No heavy drinking days were reported during the last 4 weeks of treatment for 36% of the topiramate group compared to 17% in the placebo group (OR 2.75; 1.24-6.10; NNT 5). Interestingly, however, topiramate was only effective in the 42% of patients who were homozygotic for the GRIK1 gene CC single nucleotide polymorphism at rs2832407, and this could help provide a personalized treatment option to heavy drinkers who are likely to respond well to topiramate.

Alcohol (ethanol) intoxication is diagnosed by a history of ingestion and the typical signs of slurred speech, disinhibition,and ataxia. Severe alcohol intoxication is also known as alcohol poisoning and can present as stupor or coma. C
BAC helps secure the diagnosis, but without an accurate history and exam, it is not useful in guiding treatment decisions because of patients' varying alcohol tolerance. C

Accurately detecting long-term alcohol biomarkers often leads patients to admit previously denied heavy alcohol use, making it possible to motivate them to undergo treatment for alcohol use disorder. A
Isopropyl alcohol ingestion presents clinically like ethanol ingestion; laboratory findings usually include an osmolar gap without an anion gap acidosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Response to flumazenil, positive toxicology screen
Response to naltrexone, positive toxicology screen
History of trauma, signs of trauma on examination
History of seizure, other signs of seizure (mouth trauma, positive EEG)
History of prolonged drinking, typical features on MRI
Neurological deficits, typical findings on MRI

list.listitem: Acute ethanol intoxication may present with slurred speech, disinhibition, ataxia, stupor, coma, hypotension, or shock (). Ethanol poisoning may present with altered mental status, hypothermia, respiratory compromise, hypotension, nausea/vomiting, and seizure.
Ethanol intoxication may be a factor in minor or major trauma, domestic violence, assaults including sexual, and suicide attempts.

Ethanol ingestion sufficient to cause a peak BAC of 116 +/- 18 mg/dL can cause fluid losses averaging 0.5 L at 3 hours as well as positive tilt table testing (≥30 beat/minute change in pulse or severe dizziness).

Isopropyl alcohol ingestion can occur accidentally, intentionally as an intoxicant, or to cause self-harm. It presents similarly to ethanol intoxication with inebriation, disinhibition, slurred speech, ataxia, and possibly stupor or coma. Additional findings of isopropyl alcohol ingestion include tachycardia, decreased deep tendon reflexes, hypotension, mydriasis, fever, nystagmus, abdominal cramping, muscle weakness, and in severe cases respiratory arrest. A fruity or sweet odor can sometimes be detected on the breath from ketonemia.
In all cases, it is important to determine the quantity of alcohol ingested, the time course, and if there were any coingestants.

A patient’s assessment of how intoxicated they feel is not an accurate assessment of impairment. In one study of 3112 participants with a positive BAC, nearly 40% of participants who reported being "slightly buzzed" and 16% of participants who reported "no buzz" were legally impaired for driving purposes.
While BAC is useful in the diagnosis of alcohol intoxication (), the number correlates poorly with the clinical presentation of the patient because of tolerance.
Ethanol intoxication causes an anion gap, an osmolar gap, and in severe cases acidosis ().
Breath alcohol testing using the appropriate blood to breath alcohol conversion may be a reliable and rapid screening alternative to BAC in the ED.
Transdermal alcohol testing detects alcohol expiration through skin and is under investigation as a potentially continuous and noninvasive method to monitor drinking behavior.

In addition to the directly measuring ethanol via BAC, utilizing the longer-term biomarkers of alcohol consumption to diagnose and treat alcohol use disorder cannot be overstated. These include the classic indirect markers carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT), gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT), and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) as well as the direct alcohol markers ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) in serum and urine, EtG and fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEE) in hair, and finally phosphatidylethanol (PEth) which can be tested at the bedside with a finger stick blood test.

PEth is formed on the surface of the red blood cell when ethyl alcohol reacts with phosphatidylcholine, and it can be detected for 3 or 4 weeks after chronic excessive alcohol use (including binge drinking) long after both ethanol and EtG have been metabolized in blood and urine.
Isopropyl alcohol intoxication causes an osmolar gap but not an anion gap. Acetone is the major metabolite, and finding a serum acetone or urinary ketones supports the diagnosis.
Consider screening for lead levels in consumers of illegally distilled alcohol (moonshine). C

An EKG should be used in the ED to monitor alcohol withdrawal patients for arrythmias, especially before giving medications that can lengthen the QTc interval. In one study, significantly more alcohol withdrawal patients experienced a prolonged QTc than acute coronary syndrome patients (62% vs. 46%).

CT imaging is reliably accurate at detecting cervical spine (Csp) injuries in intoxicated, blunt trauma patients [94% sensitive, 95.5% specific, and 99.5% negative predictive value (NPV) for all Csp injuries, 99.9% NPV for clinically significant injuries, and 100% NPV for unstable injuries]. This is important because alcohol intoxication often prevents clinical clearance of the Csp even after a normal CT scan, leading to prolonged immobilization.
Screening tests for alcohol use disorders include the CAGE , AUDIT-C, and in adolescents the CRAFFT.
In primary care, a CAGE score ≥3 is highly specific (LR+ 16.2) for alcohol use disorders, while in the inpatient setting a CAGE score of 4 also has a high positive likelihood ratio (LR+ 18.3).

Algorithms are helpful to manage alcohol withdrawal,
particularly those using the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) scale to measure withdrawal severity and guide treatment. Treatment of alcohol withdrawal should be followed by treatment for alcohol use disorder to improve the chances of long-term treatment.
In a patient with altered mental status, a broad differential diagnosis should be considered including infection (meningitis), occult head trauma, CVA, polysubstance use, and a postictal state.
In the unconscious patient, obtain BAC and a serum glucose level.
Patients who have ingested alcohol in an attempt at self-harm should have a psychiatric evaluation and be evaluated for the potential of alcohol withdrawal syndrome.
IV fluids are often required in patients who are hypotensive. C
Endotracheal intubation may be required in cases of decreased consciousness, respiratory compromise, and/or an inability to protect the airway from aspiration. C
Treatment of alcohol intoxication/poisoning and isopropyl alcohol ingestion is primarily supportive. C
Hemodialysis is rarely needed for isopropyl alcohol ingestion. C

In most cases of ethanol or isopropyl alcohol intoxication, supportive care and observation is all that is required. Hypotension may be treated with IV crystalloids, but pressors are sometimes also needed. Endotracheal intubation may be required in cases of severe intoxication to protect the airway or in cases of respiratory depression.
Thiamine should be administered prior to giving carbohydrate-containing food or IV fluids, and while 100mg IV is most commonly used, the optimum dose and route are unclear.
Metadoxine 900 mg IV as a one-time dose accelerates ethanol elimination and leads to faster alcohol elimination.
Neither pyridoxine IV nor flumazenil are effective in reversing alcohol-induced CNS depression.

A meta-analysis demonstrated that adding hemodialysis to the combination of conventional treatment and naloxone was beneficial in patients with acute severe alcohol intoxication byreduced hospital length of stay, coma time, time of symptom disappearance, and the incidence of some complications rate. Large scale, multicenter, and well-designed RCTs are needed.
Hemodialysis may be required for rare cases of massive isopropyl alcohol ingestion.
Patients who ingest ethanol or isopropyl alcohol in an act of self-harm should have a thorough psychiatric evaluation.
Patients who ingest isopropyl alcohol as an ethanol substitute should be offered substance use disorder treatment.

Based on the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) guideline on harmful drinking and alcohol dependence, building a trusting relationship, providing information, and encouraging family participation in treatment are key principles in caring for patients with alcohol use disorders. For persons engaging in harmful use, a psychological intervention (e.g. cognitive behavioral therapies, behavioral therapies, or social network and environment-based therapies) focused specifically on alcohol-related cognitions, behavior problems, and social networks should be offered.

Authors of two Cochrane reviews concluded that brief interventions, often involving motivational counseling, were effective in reducing self-reported alcohol consumption. Limited data showed that extended interventions on drinking offered no greater benefit, and there was no effect of brief interventions on binge drinking or drinking intensity. In hospitalized heavy alcohol users, brief interventions reduced deaths at 6 months (RR 0.42; 95% CI 0.19-0.94) and one year (RR 0.60; 95% CI 0.40-0.91).
A single motivational interview intervention for first-time driving while intoxicated arrestees did not reduce 90-day self-reported drinking behavior or increase seeking drinking treatment.

In ED patients with hazardous and harmful drinking, use of a Brief Negotiation Interview, with or without a 1-month follow-up telephone booster, reduced past 7-day alcohol consumption and 28-day binge episodes at 6 and 12 months slightly more than standard care.

In an RCT of 563 adults with alcohol and/or drug dependence, there were no significant differences in abstinence from stimulants, opioids, or heavy drinking at 12 months for patients randomized to comprehensive chronic care management vs. usual care. Similarly, authors of a Cochrane review of 15 studies (2 addressing alcohol use) found that case management vs. usual care improved referral of people with substance use disorders to community and treatment services, but did not appear to reduce substance use.

Following ED discharge of hazardous-drinking young adults, a text message intervention of short messages and feedback vs. messages alone or no intervention resulted in less self-reported binge drinking and less drinks per drinking day.
Internet-based interventions can significantly decrease alcohol consumption in the short-term among problem drinkers (LOE = 2a).

Postpartum home visits for persons with drug or alcohol use complicating their pregnancies were not found useful for any outcome measures including continued alcohol use (3 studies, 379 women), failure to enroll in a drug treatment program (2 studies, 211 women), and not breastfeeding at 6 months.
Using energy drinks with alcohol decreases some subjective perceptions of alcohol intoxication but does not reduce clinical intoxication scores or BAC.
In general, serial blood alcohol levels are not required for management. C
Observation for alcohol intoxication is indicated until clinical sobriety is established
Pediatric patients with isopropyl alcohol ingestion should be monitored for a minimum of 2 hours to assess for toxicity; signs of toxicity prompt the need for further observation.

Patients with mild-moderate transitory symptoms not requiring medications can benefit from observation in the ED because of a clinical course often completed within 24 hours and without hospitalization. Patients affected by Alcohol Use Disorder must be referred to addiction medicine for the follow-up to reduce the risk of alcohol relapse, complications related to alcohol abuse, and financial costs of hospitalization.
Patients with coingestion of other toxic substances (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, etc.) may require hospital admission.
Patients with alcoholic ketoacidosis require IV fluids and glucose.
Patients with alcohol intoxication should be hospitalized if complications such as cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension, respiratory compromise, or trauma occur.

One study demonstrated that only a small percentage of patients (1%) use critical care resources, and risk factors for serious illness (e.g. respiratory failure, sepsis, intracranial hemorrhage) include hypoglycemia (aOR 9.2), fever (aOR 7.6), hypothermia (aOR 4.2), hypotension (aOR 3.8), hypoxia (aOR 3.8), parenteral sedation (aOR 2.4), and tachycardia (aOR 1.8).

Patients with physiological alcohol dependence may need inpatient treatment using medically assisted alcohol withdrawal. The NICE guideline recommends those in acute alcohol withdrawal be admitted for detoxification, including those at high risk for developing seizures or delirium tremens. There should also be a lower threshold for admitting vulnerable populations in acute alcohol withdrawal such as those with frailty, multiple comorbidities, a cognitive impairment or learning disability, poor social support, or those younger than 18 years old.
Patients who ingest alcohol in a suicide attempt may need an inpatient psychiatric evaluation.
Patient should be offered anticraving medications like acamprosate and naltrexone as they reduce readmission rates.
Volume depletion should be corrected with IV fluids .
Hypoglycemia should be corrected after administration of thiamine.
Alcoholic ketoacidosis should be managed with IV fluids and glucose.
Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, etc.) should be corrected.
General supportive care is needed until clinical sobriety is obtained.

Most patients make a full recovery after a period of observation; however, treatment for alcohol withdrawal does not constitute longitudinal treatment for a substance use disorder. Alcohol detoxification must be considered an entry point for longitudinal care to improve the likelihood of longterm treatment of alcohol use disorders as a chronic illness. C
Patients with alcohol use disorders and acute physiological dependence on alcohol may require inpatient or outpatient treatment. B

There was no independent association between alcohol intoxication and higher in-hospital mortality in emergency patients with severe traumatic brain injury in a retrospective study, but alcohol intoxication and age at the time of injury have both been associated with lower improvement in cognitive function 2 years after traumatic brain injury
Patients admitted with alcoholic intoxication had approximately a 9-fold higher incidence of mesenteric ischemia in one retrospective cohort of 62,115 patients.

In a Dutch study of 81 intensive care units, 10.8% of admissions for intoxicants were from alcohol (792/7331) with a mean age of 38.5 years old and 69% of whom were men. In-hospital mortality was 1.4% for alcohol-related intoxicants and 2.1% for all intoxicants, while at 2 years, death for alcohol-related intoxicants increased to 7.1%.
Patients with suicidal ideation require psychiatric evaluation and possible inpatient evaluation. C

Long-term health risks include cardiovascular disease; cerebrovascular disease; liver disease; cancers of the breast, mouth, throat, esophagus, liver, and colon; mental health problems; and social problems.

In a 30-year Scottish cohort study of 5771 men, those who both smoked and drank 15+ units/week had the highest all-cause mortality (relative rate = 2.71 [95% CI 2.31-3.19] vs. never smokers who did not drink), and a quarter of these men did not survive to age 65 years.

Alcohol intoxication is a risk factor for subsequent venous thromboembolism, with a 10 year incidence for deep venous thrombosis of 9.36 per 10,000 person-years vs. 2.07 in controls and for pulmonary embolism of 4 per 10,000 person-years vs. 0.93 in controls.

Alcohol intoxication is also a risk factor for subsequent mesenteric ischemia, with a HR of 9.38 (95% CI 5.52-15.9) based on one population-based study of 62,115 patients hospitalized for alcohol intoxication.

cell.label: Does patient have signs and symptoms consistent with alcohol intoxication?
Clinically assess the degree of intoxication (see ).
Consider alternate diagnoses including other forms of intoxicants.
Observe patient until clinically sober and discharge if there is no threat to self or others.
Consider fluid resuscitation. Consider workup for alteration in mental status if present. Perform serial examinations to ensure improvement in mental status.

Consider alternate diagnoses for change in mental status. Assess for hypoglycemia. Consider administration of 100 mg of thiamine IV and fluid resuscitation. Assess airway and breathing and consider intubation. Survey for signs of occult trauma.
Assess the patient's risk factors for alcohol withdrawal syndromes and History of previous withdrawal is best predictor.

feature.caption: Correlation of Drinks, Blood Alcohol, and Symptoms with Level of Intoxication.
feature.feature_body:
Level of Intoxication Number of Drinks* Blood Alcohol Content (mg/dL) Clinical Manifestations
Mild 1-8 50-150 Talkative, loud speech, slurred speech, social inhibition, impaired sensation, ataxia, cognitive and memory impairment
Moderate 5-14 150-300 Lethargy, nausea, vomiting, reduced responsiveness, intellectual impairment
Severe 10->15 >300 Decreased respiratory drive, amnesia, hypothermia, cardiac arrhythmias, semiconscious to unconscious
*Numbers vary by sex and body weight. Adapted from Yost DA. Acute care for alcohol intoxication. Be prepared to consider clinical dilemmas. Postgrad Med 2002;112:14-16, 21-22, 25-26; and Malone D, Friedman T. Drunken patients in the general hospital: their care and management. Postgrad Med J 2005;81:161-166.

Ethanol elevated nl high
